Geometry details

Size sets the bounding-box width and height. For a circle it is the diameter; the triangle is upright and isosceles, with equal width and height. Position uses the horizontal center and bottom elevation; values are limited to the tank bounds.

The solver and drawing use the same grid-based solid boundary. Circle and triangle edges are stair-stepped; a smaller spatial step resolves their shape more closely. Geometry or grid changes restart the simulation at t = 0.

Details

A finer grid resolves smaller waves and solid-boundary details, with more computation. The time step adapts to the grid, velocity and gravity. Compare grids to explore the effect of resolution.

Model & accuracy

The 2D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations are solved on a staggered MAC grid with pressure projection. Marker particles track the free surface. Air is at atmospheric gauge pressure p = 0; solid walls use no-penetration, free-slip conditions.

This is an educational 2D cross-section of a fixed obstacle. The coarse grid, marker tracking and velocity interpolation introduce numerical error; pressure values show trends. Quantitative prediction of 3D flow, air entrainment and impact peaks requires finer models and experimental validation.

For the numerical method, see Bridson’s fluid simulation notes. For an experimental wave-impact benchmark, see Kleefsman et al. on wave impact. This demo has not been quantitatively validated against that experiment.

Free-surface time-stepping flow

  1. Identify water and solidsMarker particles locate the water; the obstacle and tank walls define solid boundaries
  2. Choose a time stepLimit each Δt using the grid, velocity and gravity
  3. Predict face velocitiesUpdate advection, viscous diffusion and gravity to obtain U*
  4. Solve the pressure Poisson equationApply atmospheric gauge pressure at the surface and no penetration at solids
  5. Project the velocityUse the pressure gradient to reduce discrete divergence in the water
  6. Record obstacle pressure and forceUse adjacent water-cell pressures to calculate upstream pressure and net pressure force
  7. Move marker particlesAdvect particles with the corrected velocity to update the free surface

Equations & boundary conditions

Incompressible water

∇·U=0 ∂U∂t+(U·∇)U=−1ρ∇p+ν∇2U+g
Details

U = (u, v), with gravity acting downward. Pressure is gauge pressure relative to the atmosphere, in Pa. Kinematic viscosity ν is in m²/s.

Pressure projection

Lhp=ρΔtDhU* Un+1=U*−ΔtρGhp
Details

Dₕ takes the discrete divergence of face velocities; Gₕ takes the gradient of adjacent cell pressures. Set p = 0 at water–air boundaries and zero normal velocity at the fixed obstacle and tank walls.

Free surface & obstacle force

dXmdt=U(Xm,t) Fx′≈−∑fpfnx,fΔsf
Details

Xₘ is a water-marker position. Integrate over all wetted solid grid faces f, with nₓ the horizontal component of the unit normal pointing from solid to water. Horizontal pressure force is in N/m of span, positive to the right. Upstream pressure is the maximum on left-facing wetted solid faces, including hydrostatic pressure.
